ChatGPT said:

Ah — then Categorical was not the problem. Your screenshot shows something more important:

The line itself has only a few vertices. So Power BI really is aggregating the monthly rows, not merely hiding the labels.

I think I see why: your YearMonth is Date/Time, and the chart is behaving oddly with that imported field. Rather than fighting Power BI's automatic date handling, create an explicit Month-Year categorical field and a numeric sort key.

1. Create a Month-Year column

In Power BI Report/Data view, select monthly_volume, then:

Table tools / Modeling → New column

Enter:

DAX
MonthYear = FORMAT(monthly_volume[YearMonth], "MMM yyyy")

Press Enter.

You should now have values such as:

Plain text
Aug 2022 Sep 2022 Oct 2022 Nov 2022 Dec 2022 Jan 2023 ...

2. Create a sorting column

Create another New column:

DAX
MonthYearSort = YEAR(monthly_volume[YearMonth]) * 100 + MONTH(monthly_volume[YearMonth])

That produces:

Plain text
202208 202209 202210 202211 ... 202401 202402 ...

This prevents Power BI from alphabetically sorting Apr, Aug, Dec, etc.

3. Tell Power BI how to sort MonthYear

Click the new:

MonthYear

column in the Data pane.

Then at the top:

Column tools → Sort by column → MonthYearSort

This step is important.

4. Replace the X-axis

Select your line chart.

Remove:

YearMonth

from X-axis.

Drag:

MonthYear

onto the X-axis.

Now Power BI has no date hierarchy to interfere with us. MonthYear is simply a category.

Keep:

Y-axis

Max of DP_Rate30

Legend

Period

5. Make sure the chart is sorted correctly

Click the ⋯ in the upper-right corner of the chart.

Choose:

Sort axis → MonthYear → Ascending

Now the chart should run:

Aug 2022 → Sep 2022 → Oct 2022 → Nov 2022 → … → Aug 2024 → Sep 2024 → …

rather than one point per year.

Why I'm recommending a separate field now

Your source data screenshot proved that the rows exist:

Plain text
Before 2022-08-01 Before 2022-09-01 Before 2022-10-01 Before 2022-11-01 Before 2022-12-01 Before 2023-01-01 ...

So don't change Power Query or Python.

The cleanest solution is to stop letting Power BI interpret YearMonth as a date hierarchy at all. MonthYear becomes a categorical display field, while MonthYearSort quietly keeps everything chronological.

After doing this, you should have dozens of monthly points, not four. If you still get four after using MonthYear, then something else is filtering the visual, and we'll check that next.

You said:

What if I want to compare the dp rate by month by period

ChatGPT said:

Yes. If by “compare DP rate by month by Period” you mean:

Compare January Before vs January During, February Before vs February During, etc.

then that's a different chart from the chronological MonthYear chart, and it's useful for your project because it helps reveal seasonal differences while comparing the policy periods.

Build this chart

Create a new Line chart and use:

Power BI areaField
X-axisMonth name
Y-axisDP_Rate30
LegendPeriod

You want the result conceptually to be:

Plain text
Before During Jan ●-------------● Feb ●-----------------● Mar ●-----------● Apr ●----------------● ... Dec ●-------------●

More precisely, Power BI will draw two lines across Jan–Dec: one for Before and one for During.

1. Create MonthName

Select monthly_volume → New column:

DAX
MonthName = FORMAT(monthly_volume[YearMonth], "MMM")

That gives:

Jan, Feb, Mar, Apr ... Dec

2. Create MonthNumber

Create another column:

DAX
MonthNumber = MONTH(monthly_volume[YearMonth])

Then select MonthName → Column tools → Sort by column → MonthNumber.

Otherwise Power BI will happily give you Apr, Aug, Dec, Feb... because apparently the alphabet is a perfectly reasonable calendar.

3. The Y-axis needs special attention

For this comparison, I would not use MAX(DP_Rate30).

Suppose you have:

Plain text
Period YearMonth DP_Rate30 Before Jan 2023 223 Before Jan 2024 339 During Jan 2025 212 During Jan 2026 245

When X-axis = Jan, we're intentionally grouping multiple Januaries together.

So we need to decide what statistic represents January during each period.

A straightforward descriptive comparison is:

Average of DP_Rate30

Configure:

X-axis

MonthName

Y-axis

Average of DP_Rate30

Legend

Period

Now Power BI calculates approximately:

January Before=Jan 2023 rate+Jan 2024 rate2\text{January Before} = \frac{\text{Jan 2023 rate}+\text{Jan 2024 rate}}{2}January Before=2Jan 2023 rate+Jan 2024 rate​

and separately:

January During=Jan 2025 rate+Jan 2026 rate2\text{January During} = \frac{\text{Jan 2025 rate}+\text{Jan 2026 rate}}{2}January During=2Jan 2025 rate+Jan 2026 rate​

But there's an important statistical issue

For your project, I'd prefer a weighted rate rather than simply averaging monthly DP_Rate30 values, especially because your observation windows contain partial months.

You already have PermitCount and ExposureDays. So the period/month rate can be calculated from the underlying totals:

DP Rate30=∑PermitCount∑ExposureDays×30\text{DP Rate30} = \frac{\sum PermitCount} {\sum ExposureDays} \times 30DP Rate30=∑ExposureDays∑PermitCount​×30

Create this measure:

DAX
DP Rate per 30 Days = DIVIDE( SUM(monthly_volume[PermitCount]), SUM(monthly_volume[ExposureDays]) ) * 30

Then build:

AreaUse
X-axisMonthName
Y-axisDP Rate per 30 Days measure
LegendPeriod

This lets the filter context do the work. At January + Before, for example, Power BI sums the relevant January permit counts and exposure days and then calculates the normalized rate.

I would actually keep both charts

They answer different questions:

Chronological chart

MonthYear → DP Rate → Period

Answers:

How did residential DP activity change over time?

Month-of-year comparison

MonthName → DP Rate per 30 Days → Period

Answers:

For the same calendar month, how does normalized DP activity differ between Before and During periods?

That second one is particularly useful for your project because development-permit activity can be seasonal. Comparing January with January, February with February, etc. helps separate the apparent policy-period difference from ordinary month-of-year variation.

One caution: if the During period has fewer years of observations than Before, say that explicitly in your analysis. The rate normalization handles different exposure days, but it doesn't magically make a short observation period statistically equivalent to a longer one.

You said:

powerbi statically different

ChatGPT said:

If you mean “Can Power BI test whether the DP rates are statistically different between the Before and During periods?” — yes. That would be a strong addition to your Data 110 analysis.

But Power BI's normal visuals give you descriptive statistics; they don't automatically establish statistical significance.

For your project, I would separate the analysis into:

QuestionAnalysis
Are average DP rates different?Mean/median by Period
How large is the difference?Absolute and % difference
Is the difference statistically significant?Hypothesis test
Could the apparent difference just be seasonal?Compare month-of-year / control for month
Are the distributions different?Box plot / distribution visualization
How uncertain is the estimate?95% confidence intervals

For example, your hypothesis could be:

H0:μBefore=μDuringH_0:\mu_{\text{Before}}=\mu_{\text{During}}H0​:μBefore​=μDuring​

versus:

HA:μBefore≠μDuringH_A:\mu_{\text{Before}}\ne\mu_{\text{During}}HA​:μBefore​=μDuring​

But there's an important issue with your particular dataset: these are monthly observations over time. January 2023 isn't necessarily independent of February 2023, and development permits have seasonality. A simple t-test treating every month as an unrelated observation can therefore be misleading.

For your mini-capstone, a sensible approach would be to use Power BI for descriptive comparisons and visualization, and Python for the statistical test. You can then bring the Python results back into Power BI.

I would specifically analyze Before vs During using DP_Rate30, report the mean difference and 95% CI, and examine seasonality/month effects rather than relying solely on a raw two-sample t-test.

If by “statistically different” you meant how to make Power BI calculate whether Before and During are statistically significantly different, I can walk you through that next using your actual monthly_volume data.
